title: Weight reduction in asthma programme with tirzepatide
official: Weight Reduction in Asthma Programme with Tirzepatide (WRAPT): clinical efficacy and mechanisms of action
summary:
Background and study aims 
Asthma and overweight are both common health problems in the UK, and they often occur together. Having asthma can make it harder to stay active, and some asthma treatments involve steroids, which can make weight loss more difficult. This can lead to a cycle where asthma and weight problems each make the other worse. Research shows that people with asthma are more likely to be overweight than people without asthma. We also know that losing weight can help improve asthma symptoms. However, losing weight can be very difficult. Tirzepatide is a medication that helps people lose weight and may also improve asthma. Early studies suggest it may reduce asthma attacks. 
We want to find out whether tirzepatide can improve asthma. To do this, we will look at asthma symptoms (using a questionnaire), breathing tests, body weight and body fat, and chemicals in the blood that are linked to inflammation and body fat. We also want to understand how any improvements happen, for example, whether they are due to weight loss or changes in inflammation. 

Who can participate?
Patients aged 18 years and over who have both asthma and overweight

What does the study involve? 
Eligibility will be assessed against asthma control, body mass index, medical history, smoking history and alcohol consumption. At the start of the study, participants will complete questionnaires. They will have height, weight, waist size, and body fat measured. Participants will give blood samples (to check inflammation and ensure the medicine is safe). They will also have breathing tests to assess lung health. Half the participants will inject tirzepatide treatment, the other half a dummy medicine, as a weekly injection for 1 year. All will have an equal chance of having the study medication. At the end of the study, all tests and measurements will be repeated. This will help us understand whether tirzepatide improves asthma, weight, breathing, or inflammation. There will be a mixture of hospital and at-home time points.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
We cannot promise that this study will help you. However, the information we learn from it might help us treat people in the future who have a higher weight and have asthma that is hard to control.
The spirometry breathing tests may cause chest discomfort or tightness. If this happens, it will wear off after a minute or two, and participants will be able to take their reliever medication to help. Research staff will check with participants before the test commences to ensure there are no clinical reasons the test is unsuitable for the participant.
For the nitric oxide test, participants will have to breathe out in a controlled manner into a tube. Sometimes this is a bit difficult to do. However, the test is not painful or uncomfortable.
It may be necessary for participants to travel to the hospital for visits in addition to their routine clinic visits. Spirometry, static volume lung function tests, FeNO assessment, and venous blood sampling for research biomarkers need to be undertaken in clinical research or other appropriate facilities (at baseline, week 20, and week 52). If more convenient and appropriate, safety bloods can be collected in primary care at 8 and 36 weeks and reported to the research site. Questionnaires will be completed online or on paper, at home or in another suitable setting. Weight, waist, and hip measurements will be undertaken at home and the results captured electronically, or on paper, at home. 
The blood tests may cause discomfort and bruising. The questionnaires will take between 15 and 30 minutes to complete. We will not be asking about any sensitive information.
Participants will need to inject medication or a placebo once a week for 52 weeks. As doses are self-administered by injection, this may cause discomfort at the injection site. Participants will be trained how to inject the IMP at their baseline visit. While tirzepatide has some known side effects, part of the study is identifying the maximum tolerated dose with doses escalating through the study, starting at 2.5 mg. Adverse events will be closely monitored, and dose escalation can be paused or de-escalated based on any side effects that cannot be tolerated. If the participant experiences adverse events, they will be encouraged to discuss this with their clinical care team so the most appropriate course of action can be taken. Adverse event information will be collected for safety reporting.

Where is the study run from? 
University of East Anglia (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
December 2026 to January 2028

Who is funding the study? 
NIHR Efficacy and Mechanism Evaluation Programme (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Prof. Andrew Wilson, A.M.Wilson@uea.ac.uk
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged ≥18 years
2. Diagnosis of asthma as per British Thoracic Society (BTS)/Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN)/National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines [NG245] with at least moderate dose maintenance and reliever therapy (MART)
3. Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ-7) of more than 1.5 (indicates poor control)
4. Body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m² for non-Asian population or BMI ≥27 kg/m² for Asian population
5. Stable disease, as evidenced by a lack of change in asthma therapy or antibiotics within the last 6 weeks, with appropriate asthma management including biological therapies if appropriate
Exclusion criteria:
1. Significant cardiac disease, respiratory disease, or other cause for breathlessness other than asthma.
2. Having had an upper or lower respiratory tract infection requiring antibiotics within 4 weeks of randomisation.
3. History of type I diabetes or history of type II diabetes mellitus receiving treatment with GLP-1 RA and GIP/GLP-1 RA or dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitor hypoglycaemics (gliptins) or with proliferative diabetic retinopathy or diabetic macular oedema or severe non-proliferative retinopathy that requires acute treatment or are uncontrolled (HbA1c >10% within 3 months prior to screening).
4. Current smoker or more than 15 pack-year smoking history.
5. Consumption of more than 21 units of alcohol per week, known or suspected alcohol or recreational drug abuse, including oral, inhaled or injection drugs in the year prior to screening.
6. Have a prior or planned surgical, endoscopic or device-based treatment for obesity.
7. Taking medication known to induce weight gain within the past 90 days before screening such as atypical antipsychotic and mood stabilizers.
8. Treatment with tricyclic antidepressants that has been initiated less than 6 months before screening and/or has treatment with tricyclic antidepressants that have undergone a change in dosage or regime in the 6 months prior to screening.
9. Other weight loss or gain therapy-specific contraindications as judged by the study clinician.
10. Have a self-reported change in body weight >5 kg within 3 months prior to screening
11.	Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2 or endocrinological disorders resulting in obesity.
12.	History of malignant neoplasms within the past 5 years prior to screening. Basal and squamous cell skin cancer and any carcinoma in situ are allowed.
13.	Personal history of acute pancreatitis 180 days before screening or chronic pancreatitis.
14. Clinically significant gastric emptying abnormality or chronically taking medication adversely affecting GI motility
15.	Uncontrolled hypertension (systolic blood pressure ≥160 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥100 mmHg).
16. Severe renal impairment measured as glomerular infiltration rate (eGFR <15 ml/min 1.73 m²).
17.	Uncontrolled thyroid disease defined as have a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) outside of 0.4 to 6.0 mIU/L at the screening visit.
18.	History of stroke, unstable angina, acute coronary syndrome, congestive heart failure New York Heart Association class III-IV within the preceding 3 months.
19. Untreated clinically significant arrhythmias.
20. Pregnant or breastfeeding women, or women who intend to become pregnant.
21.	Women of Childbearing Potential (WOCBP) not using a highly effective form of contraceptive. Pregnancy tests will be required at trial start and at 12 weeks. Highly effective forms of contraception defined as: methods of birth control which result in a low failure rate (i.e., less than 1% per year) when used consistently and correctly such, as implants, injectables, combined oral contraceptives, progesterone-only oral contraceptives associated with inhibiting ovulation, some intrauterine devices (IUDs), intrauterine hormone-releasing system (IUS) or hormonal coil, sexual abstinence (defined as refraining from heterosexual intercourse during the entire period of risk associated with study treatments), sterilisation or vasectomized partner (for which the vasectomised partner has received medical assessment of the surgical success). This will apply to all women under 55 years of age unless they are confirmed to be postmenopausal or infertile. Postmenopausal is defined as at least 12 months of spontaneous amenorrhea for women over 50 years or 24 months spontaneous amenorrhoea for women under 50 years. Infertility is defined as females who have had a hysterectomy, bilateral salpingectomy, bilateral oophorectomy or other confirmed cause of infertility at least 6 weeks prior to enrolment.
22. Known or suspected hypersensitivity to tirzepatide, placebo or any of the excipients involved in their formulation.
23. Participation in another clinical intervention trial.
24. Any additional factor, which in the investigator’s opinion, might jeopardise the participant’s safety or compliance with the trial protocol.
25. Patients unable to give written informed consent.
